lesson.title: Packed to the Rafters: Life in the Tenements
lesson.summary: To house the flood of newcomers pouring into industrial cities, landlords built cramped multi-family tenement buildings that offered cheap shelter at the cost of light, air, sanitation, and safety.
lesson.body:
A tenement was a multistory building divided into small apartments, typically packed with far more residents than it was ever designed to hold comfortably. Tenements became the dominant form of housing in dense immigrant neighborhoods like Manhattan's Lower East Side, a direct consequence of the explosive urban growth described in the story of Urbanization, since the huge influx of new city residents created enormous demand for housing that was cheap and close to factory jobs.

One especially common design became known as the dumbbell tenement, named for the shape of its floor plan, narrowed in the middle to create a thin air shaft between adjacent buildings. This design became standard in New York after an 1879 design competition and the New York State Tenement House Act of that same year, which required that every room have some access to a window or air shaft. In practice, these narrow shafts let in little real light or fresh air and often became dumping grounds for garbage, creating serious fire hazards instead of solving the problem they were meant to fix.

Daily life in the tenements was crowded and difficult. Apartments frequently had no direct sunlight, toilets were often shared among many families in a hallway or courtyard, and many families took in boarders or did piecework, such as sewing, inside their already tiny apartments just to afford the rent. Disease, especially tuberculosis, spread easily in such crowded, poorly ventilated conditions, and fire remained a constant danger.

These conditions reached a wide, largely middle class audience in 1890, when the Danish immigrant journalist and photographer Jacob Riis published How the Other Half Lives, using flash photography to document tenement interiors that most comfortable New Yorkers had never seen firsthand.

Public exposure and continued pressure eventually led to the New York Tenement House Act of 1901, which imposed much stricter requirements on new buildings, including wider air shafts, indoor plumbing, and better fireproofing. It marked one of the first major building code reforms driven by public health and social reform concerns, a small preview of the broader wave of reform that would define the Progressive Era just ahead.
